description:
Three examples written today (fft.exs, image_ops.exs, geohash_crc.exs) needed to reject bad input (a non-power-of-two length, odd dimensions, a bad precision or alphabet byte) and had no way to say so: each works around it with `_ = alloc(f64, -1)` or `div(1, 0)` to force an exception whose message is about something else. A kernel author would write `raise ArgumentError, "n must be a power of two"` first, and it has an exact Elixir meaning.

Scope: `raise Module, "literal message"` and `raise Module` (default message), `Module` in {ArgumentError, ArithmeticError}; `raise "msg"` as RuntimeError; the message is a string literal (interpolation is rejected with a rewrite: "put the value in Elixir, before or after the call"). Used as a statement anywhere a statement goes (inside if/cond/case arms too), and as the tail of a reduce_while fn arm? (no: keep statements only; a `raise` as an expression value is rejected with the hint "raise is a statement"). Natively: defk_fail with a new kind per module (the existing DEFK_E_ARG/ARITH kinds for ArgumentError/ArithmeticError, a new one for RuntimeError) and the literal message; Elixir mode: the raise itself. The normalised reason (Defk.Test.reason/1) for a user raise is {:user, message} so agreement compares the message. In a select-compiled if/cond, an arm that raises is not speculated (the arm has a statement, so select?/1 already refuses it).

Tests: both modes via assert_agrees for each module and the default message; raise inside a yielding loop under forced yields; raise in a case arm; the interpolation rewrite; raise as a value rejected. Docs: docs/language.md section 7 entry and the error section regenerated; README "Language" bullet; update the three examples to use it (fft.exs, image_ops.exs, geohash_crc.exs) and drop their workaround comments.

Done when: the three examples raise with a real message, agreement holds, and the suite is green.
title: raise in a kernel: raise ArgumentError, "literal message" and raise ArithmeticError
